framed_question: How can this DRF skill be improved? What's missing, weak, redundant, or could be better structured? Consider: clarity, completeness, triggering accuracy, examples, edge cases, anti-patterns, organization, and real-world effectiveness.

advisors.name: The Contrarian
advisors.response: This skill has a fatal structural problem: it's a routing document, not a skill. The SKILL.md is essentially a table of contents pointing to eight reference files that the agent must then read. This means the skill triggers, adds tokens for the routing layer, and then the agent reads the actual content anyway. The 'Critical Rules' section is the most valuable part of the entire SKILL.md — 14 hard-won gotchas that save real debugging time — but it's buried mid-file and reads like a random grab bag. There's no prioritization. Rule #1 (fields/exclude mandatory) affects every single serializer. Rule #11 (throttling race conditions) is an edge case. They're mixed together as if equally important. The 'When Not To Use This Skill' section is good but incomplete — it doesn't mention FastAPI, which is the #1 confusion point I see in practice: agents reaching for DRF when the project is actually using FastAPI or Django Ninja. The cross-domain routing table has a duplicate entry (Serializer with permissions appears twice). That's a copy-paste error that signals nobody reviewed this carefully. The skill also has zero guidance on common anti-patterns: no mention of N+1 queries via serializers, no warning about massive querysets in ListAPIView, no guidance on when to use SerializerMethodField vs annotation. These are the mistakes that actually hurt production systems.

advisors.name: The First Principles Thinker
advisors.response: What is this skill actually trying to accomplish? The stated goal is to help an agent correctly implement DRF APIs. But the skill assumes the agent knows what DRF is, which reference to read, and how to map a real-world task to the routing table. The fundamental question is: what does an agent get wrong when it DOESN'T have this skill? The answer: it hallucinates DRF APIs, uses outdated patterns (pre-3.0 style), misses security implications, and writes broken tests. The current skill addresses hallucination by providing reference files, but it does nothing for the other failure modes. The 'Critical Rules' section is the closest thing to preventing real mistakes, but it's a flat list with no context on WHY each rule exists or what failure it prevents. A first-principles rebuild would restructure around failure modes: 'Your serializer will break if...' / 'Your view will be insecure if...' / 'Your tests will be fake if...'. The reference architecture is sound — splitting into domain files is the right call. But the entry point should be a decision tree, not a flat table. The agent faces a task like 'add pagination to an existing endpoint' — it needs to know which file to read AND what the common pitfalls are. Currently it gets the routing but not the pitfalls unless it reads the reference file first.

advisors.name: The Expansionist
advisors.response: This skill is leaving enormous value on the table by being purely reactive. It waits for the agent to have a DRF question, then routes to a reference. What if the skill could proactively catch DRF anti-patterns in code review? Add a 'Code Review Checklist' section that lets the agent audit existing DRF code: 'Are there ModelSerializers without explicit fields? Are there ListAPIViews without pagination? Are there ViewSets with unrestricted destroy actions?' This turns the skill from a reference lookup into an active quality gate. Second, the skill should own the DRF + Django integration boundary more aggressively. The line between DRF and pure Django is where the worst bugs live — CSRF issues, session auth confusion, ORM queries inside serializers. The skill should have a dedicated section on 'DRF-Django boundary pitfalls' that covers request lifecycle differences, CSRF implications of token auth vs session auth, and queryset evaluation timing. Third, there's no mention of DRF's schema generation (OpenAPI/Swagger). In 2024+, most teams need API documentation. The skill should route schema questions to the right reference or explicitly own that domain. Finally, add a 'Performance' section: select_related/prefetch_related in ViewSet querysets, serializer depth control, pagination as a performance tool — not just a UX feature.

advisors.name: The Outsider
advisors.response: I have no idea what this project is or what DRF stands for. Reading the SKILL.md, I see 'Django REST Framework' in the title but the first paragraph is dense with jargon: 'serializers, fields, relations, validators, views, APIView, @api_view, generics, viewsets, routers, @action, authentication, permissions, throttling, filtering, pagination, parsers, renderers, content negotiation.' That's a wall of nouns with no explanation. If I'm a fresh agent instance that hasn't seen DRF before, this doesn't orient me. The 'Quick Start' section says 'Identify the primary domain of the task' — but how do I identify a domain if I don't know what these terms mean? The routing table uses file names like 'serializers-fields.md' which are opaque. What does 'internals.md' contain? The description says 'Dispatch flow, parsing pipeline, versioning, schemas' — but that's hidden behind the table. The 'Critical Rules' section is actually the most readable part because each rule is self-contained and explains a concrete failure. More of that style would help. The skill also assumes I know what 'loading @django' means — this is framework-specific jargon for skill loading that isn't explained anywhere in the SKILL.md itself. A two-sentence glossary at the top would transform this from an insider document to something an outsider can use.

advisors.name: The Executor
advisors.response: The fastest improvement: move the Critical Rules to the top of SKILL.md, above the Quick Start. These 14 rules are the highest-density value in the entire skill — they prevent real bugs. Right now an agent has to read past the routing table, the when-not-to-use section, and the quick start before it hits the rules that matter. Second: fix the duplicate cross-domain entry. It's a one-line fix and it signals quality. Third: add a 'Minimal Example' section — one complete ViewSet + Serializer + Router registration that works end-to-end. Agents pattern-match from examples faster than from routing tables. Fourth: the 'Output Expectations' section says 'Name the reference files used' — this is meta-guidance for the agent's output, but it's buried. Make it a one-line callout at the top. Fifth: add a single anti-pattern — the N+1 query in serializer relations — as a concrete example under Critical Rules. It's the #1 production performance issue with DRF and it's not mentioned anywhere. These five changes take 30 minutes to implement and would measurably reduce DRF-related bugs in generated code. The reference files are fine as-is for now — the problem is the entry point, not the content.

peer_reviews.strongest: The Executor — it identifies the highest-leverage change (moving Critical Rules to top) and backs it with a concrete, prioritized list of fixes. The five-step plan is actionable without being overwhelming.
peer_reviews.biggest_blind_spot: The Contrarian correctly identifies the duplicate entry and the N+1 gap, but its tone undermines the valid points. It calls the skill 'a random grab bag' when the Critical Rules are actually well-crafted — they just need better positioning. The FastAPI confusion point is strong though.
peer_reviews.what_all_missed: None of the advisors addressed the skill's lack of version awareness. DRF has had significant changes across versions (3.x to 3.14+), and the skill doesn't specify which version it targets or note version-specific gotchas. This matters because agents may apply deprecated patterns.

peer_reviews.strongest: The First Principles Thinker — it correctly identifies that the skill is a routing document and asks what failure modes it actually prevents. The 'failure modes' reframe is the most intellectually honest assessment and would lead to the best structural improvement.
peer_reviews.biggest_blind_spot: The Expansionist's code review checklist idea is exciting but scope creep. The skill is already 150+ lines in SKILL.md alone, plus 8 reference files. Adding a full code review section would bloat it beyond what an agent reads in a single turn. The idea should be a separate skill, not bolted onto this one.
peer_reviews.what_all_missed: Nobody mentioned that the skill has no eval or test suite. For a skill that's supposed to prevent DRF bugs, there's no way to verify it actually works. Where are the evals that test whether an agent with this skill produces correct DRF code vs. one without it?

peer_reviews.strongest: The Contrarian — despite the aggressive tone, it surfaces the most concrete bugs: the duplicate routing entry, the missing N+1 warning, the missing FastAPI exclusion. These are real defects that should be fixed immediately.
peer_reviews.biggest_blind_spot: The Outsider's critique of jargon is valid but impractical. This is a specialist skill for a specialist framework. Simplifying 'serializers' and 'viewsets' for newcomers would make the skill useless for its actual audience — agents who need DRF reference material, not a DRF tutorial. The skill should assume framework knowledge.
peer_reviews.what_all_missed: The skill's description frontmatter is its triggering mechanism, and none of the advisors evaluated it. The description is comprehensive but could be tightened — 'building, securing, or fixing REST APIs powered by rest_framework' is the key trigger phrase, but it's buried in a long sentence. Triggering accuracy depends on this text.

peer_reviews.strongest: The Executor and The Contrarian together provide the most complete picture. Executor identifies the structural fix (rules first), Contrarian identifies the content gaps (N+1, FastAPI). Combined, they give a clear improvement path.
peer_reviews.biggest_blind_spot: The First Principles Thinker's 'failure mode' restructuring idea is theoretically elegant but would require rewriting all 8 reference files to follow a consistent pattern. That's a massive refactor for uncertain benefit. The current file-per-domain structure is fine; the entry point is what needs work.
peer_reviews.what_all_missed: The skill has no guidance on DRF's relationship with Django's async views. DRF 3.14+ added async support, but most of the skill's patterns (ViewSet, generics) are synchronous. An agent trying to use DRF in an async Django project would get no help here.

peer_reviews.strongest: The Expansionist's DRF-Django boundary section idea is the single most valuable addition nobody else mentioned. The CSRF/session/auth confusion at the DRF-Django boundary is the #1 source of security bugs in Django API projects, and the skill currently says nothing about it.
peer_reviews.biggest_blind_spot: The Executor's 'minimal example' suggestion sounds good but is a trap. A minimal example becomes a cargo-cult pattern that agents copy without understanding. The Critical Rules approach (explaining what breaks) is more robust than the example approach (showing what works).
peer_reviews.what_all_missed: The skill references 'tests/test_validate_refs.py' implicitly through the repo's AGENTS.md, but the SKILL.md itself says nothing about how to verify the skill's own accuracy. A skill about API testing should mention that its own references need periodic validation against the actual DRF source code.

chairman_verdict.agrees: All five advisors agree the Critical Rules section is the most valuable content and needs better positioning. Four of five agree the skill is missing performance/N+1 guidance. All agree the duplicate cross-domain entry is a defect. Three agree the skill needs better DRF-Django boundary guidance. Three agree the entry point (SKILL.md) is a routing layer that adds tokens without adding proportional value.
chairman_verdict.clashes: The Contrarian wants the skill to be more aggressive about anti-patterns; The Outsider wants it to be more accessible to newcomers. These are in tension — adding glossary content for outsiders would bloat the skill for its target audience. The Expansionist wants to add code review and schema generation; Reviewer 2 correctly flags this as scope creep. The First Principles Thinker wants a full restructuring around failure modes; The Executor argues for targeted surgical fixes to the existing structure.
chairman_verdict.blind_spots: (1) No advisor evaluated the frontmatter description for triggering accuracy — this is the skill's actual interface with the agent runtime. (2) No advisor mentioned DRF async support or version targeting. (3) The skill has no self-validation mechanism — no evals, no test that references match real DRF APIs. (4) The skill doesn't address the DRF-Django CSRF/session boundary, which is a real security concern.
chairman_verdict.recommendation: Execute a surgical improvement in three phases. Phase 1 (immediate): Move Critical Rules to the top of SKILL.md, fix the duplicate cross-domain entry, add N+1 query warning as Critical Rule #15. Phase 2 (short-term): Add a 'DRF-Django Boundary' section covering CSRF implications, request lifecycle differences, and queryset evaluation timing. Tighten the frontmatter description for triggering accuracy. Phase 3 (medium-term): Create an eval suite that verifies the skill produces correct DRF code for common tasks (serializer with nested write, secured ViewSet, paginated list).
chairman_verdict.first_step: Move the Critical Rules section from its current position (after 'When Not To Use This Skill') to immediately after the Quick Start section, before the Reference Map. This is a pure reorganization that doesn't add content but ensures agents see the gotchas before they start reading references. Fix the duplicate 'Serializer with permissions' cross-domain entry in the same edit.
